questions.prompt: What is a Fabric tenant?
options: The top-level governance boundary in Microsoft Fabric, mapped 1:1 to the organization's Microsoft Entra ID
The compute and governance unit that a workspace is assigned to, with its own region and admins
A grouping of workspaces by business area, used for organization-wide discovery
A per-item permission grant layered on top of a workspace role
The container every Fabric item lives inside, governed by Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer roles
A searchable, domain-filterable view of items across the tenant's OneLake
questions.explain: A Fabric tenant is the top-level governance boundary, mapped 1:1 to the organization's Microsoft Entra ID; everything else this course covers — domains, capacities, workspaces, items — nests inside that one boundary.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a capacity, not a tenant. A capacity is the compute and governance unit a workspace is assigned to, with its own region and its own admins separate from tenant admins — but a single tenant can contain many capacities. Confusing the two is exactly the mix-up Lesson 2 draws the line against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Fabric tenant maps 1:1 to the organization's Microsoft ________ — the same identity tenant Power BI already uses.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 states the tenant maps 1:1 to Microsoft Entra ID. If an organization has one Entra ID, it has exactly one Fabric tenant, and every governance structure this course covers lives inside that one boundary.

questions.prompt: Match each Fabric governance structure to what it actually controls.
right: The compute and governance unit a workspace is assigned to, with its own region and admins
One of four access levels (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) deciding what a person can do inside one workspace
The top-level governance boundary, mapped 1:1 to the organization's Microsoft Entra ID
A grouping of workspaces by business area, for organization-wide discovery and governance
questions.explain: The tenant is the top-level boundary mapped to Entra ID; a capacity is the compute/governance unit with its own region and admins; a domain groups workspaces by business area for discovery; and a workspace role is the four-level access grant that applies inside one workspace — four distinct layers, narrower at each step except domain, which cuts across capacities rather than nesting inside them.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of assigning a workspace into a domain through the admin portal in the correct order, per Lesson 4.
items: Open the admin portal's Domains page and select the domain to assign a workspace into
Select Assign workspaces to open the three-method dialog
Choose one of the three assignment methods: by workspace name, by workspace admin, or by capacity
Confirm the assignment and see the workspace appear in that domain's workspace list
questions.explain: The path runs Domains page, select the target domain, open Assign workspaces, then pick one of the three methods Lesson 4 names — by name, by workspace admin, or by capacity — before the workspace actually lands in that domain's list.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four Fabric workspace roles, per Lesson 5.
options: A Contributor can create and edit content but cannot manage who has access to the workspace at all
A Member can add and edit content, and can manage some access by adding people at the Member role or below
A Viewer can create new items but cannot edit existing ones
An Admin can manage every item, manage access including adding other Admins, and delete the workspace itself
Contributor and Member grant identical access, since both can build and edit items
questions.explain: A Contributor can build and edit but never touches the access list; a Member can build and edit and can also add people at the Member role or below; an Admin has the broadest control, including deleting the workspace itself. A Viewer is read-only — it cannot create or edit anything at all, not even a restricted subset. Contributor and Member are not identical: the one real difference, and the one Lesson 5 says trips people up most, is that Member can manage some access and Contributor cannot.

questions.prompt: A finance team needs a BI-facing dataset where the shape of the data can never change out from under a published report, while an engineering team needs a place to land semi-structured data before it's fully modeled. Which Fabric item type should each team be steered toward, and why?
options: The finance team should get a Warehouse, because it's schema-on-write and enforces a defined structure; the engineering team should get a Lakehouse, because it's schema-on-read and doesn't lock in structure at write time
Both teams should use a Lakehouse, since Lakehouse and Warehouse both store data in OneLake and are functionally interchangeable
The finance team should get a Lakehouse, because Spark enforces a stricter schema than T-SQL; the engineering team should get a Warehouse, because it's more flexible for raw data
Either item works for either team, since schema enforcement is a workspace-role setting, not a property of the item type
questions.explain: A Warehouse is schema-on-write — a full T-SQL engine with an enforced, defined schema that a BI consumer can rely on not shifting underneath their report. A Lakehouse is schema-on-read and Spark-oriented, giving engineering teams room to work with raw or semi-structured data before it's fully modeled. Lesson 7 frames the choice exactly this way: BI and reporting consumers toward a Warehouse, engineering and data science teams needing flexibility toward a Lakehouse.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about OneLake security, per Lesson 8.
options: OneLake security is a separate, more fine-grained layer than workspace roles — it controls which rows and columns someone sees once they're already inside an item
Row security in OneLake security is defined as an actual SQL WHERE-clause filter, evaluated at read time
OneLake security only restricts what a user sees inside the Fabric portal UI — a notebook or the SQL analytics endpoint bypasses it
A Viewer with no OneLake security role applied still sees every row of every table they have workspace access to
Column security and row security are configured on the same tab, since Fabric treats them as one combined rule set
questions.explain: OneLake security narrows visibility inside an item someone can already open, with row security defined as a literal SQL WHERE clause evaluated at read time. A Viewer with no OneLake security role still sees every row, since nothing has narrowed it yet. Enforcement is explicitly not UI-only — Lesson 8 states it's evaluated wherever the data is actually read, including a Spark notebook or the SQL analytics endpoint. Row security and column security are also separate tabs, not one combined rule set.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every Lakehouse ships with a built-in ________ role that gives anyone with the item's ReadAll permission access to all of its data, silently overriding a narrower data access role unless it's removed or edited.
questions.explain: Lesson 10 calls this out specifically: adding someone to a narrowly scoped data access role does nothing if they're still covered by DefaultReader — they keep the broader access until DefaultReader itself is removed or edited down.

questions.prompt: Match each Fabric access-control layer to the question it actually answers, per Lesson 10's three-layer framework.
right: Which specific rows within a table a role's members can see, enforced wherever the data is read
What someone can do — manage, write, read — across an entire workspace
Which specific tables or folders inside one item a person with limited standing can see at all
Whether someone who isn't a workspace member can access one specific item as a whole
questions.explain: Workspace roles are the control-plane layer governing what someone can do across a whole workspace. Item-level Manage permissions is also control plane, but confined to one item for someone who isn't even a workspace member. OneLake data access roles are data plane, scoping visibility down to specific tables and folders inside one item. Row security is the finest grain of all — filtering specific rows within an already-visible table, enforced at read time regardless of which tool reads it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating a OneLake data access role in the correct order, per the New role wizard in Lesson 10.
items: Open Manage OneLake security on a Lakehouse and select New to start the wizard
Name the role and choose its permission (Read or ReadWrite)
On the Data step, choose Selected data and use Edit to check specific tables and folders
On the Member step, add members by hand or use Advanced configuration for permission-group-based virtual membership
questions.explain: The wizard runs Role (name and permission) first, then Data — where choosing Selected data instead of All data is what makes the role fine-grained — then Member, where membership is either typed in by hand or built dynamically through Advanced configuration's permission-group-based virtual membership, exactly the three-step order Lesson 10 walks through.

questions.prompt: A workspace enables shortcut caching with a 28-day retention period. Three weeks later, the external source behind a shortcut revokes a user's access and deletes the underlying file. What does Lesson 9 say actually happens to that user's view of the cached copy?
options: The cached copy inside OneLake isn't automatically cleared by the source's deletion or access revocation — it can remain readable from the cache for up to the remaining retention window
The cache is automatically invalidated the instant the source file is deleted or access is revoked, since Fabric continuously syncs cache state with the source
Caching only stores metadata, never the actual data, so there's nothing left to see regardless of the source's state
The shortcut itself breaks immediately and the folder disappears from the Lakehouse the moment the source changes
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit that a deletion or access revocation at the source doesn't automatically clear what's already cached — cached shortcut data is a second copy, held inside the workspace, that exists independently of the source for up to the configured 1-28 day retention window. That's exactly why it's called out as a governance gap a retention policy needs to account for, not just a performance detail.

questions.prompt: What is row-level security (RLS) in a Power BI semantic model?
options: Model-level security that filters which rows a role sees, defined with a DAX filter expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE per row
An item-level sharing grant that decides whether someone can open a semantic model at all
A workspace role that restricts which items inside a workspace a person can see
A SQL WHERE-clause filter applied to a Lakehouse table through OneLake security's Data step
A Purview classification tag that determines a file's encryption and content-marking behavior
A tenant setting that blocks saving an unlabeled item until a classification is applied
questions.explain: RLS is model-level security defined in Power BI Desktop's Manage roles window — a DAX filter expression per role that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE for every row, and only rows that return TRUE stay visible to that role's members. It follows the data into every report, app, and Q&A experience built on the model, regardless of who built the report.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes OneLake security's row security from Lesson 8 — a genuinely real Fabric feature, but it's a SQL WHERE-clause filter scoped to a Lakehouse or Warehouse's OneLake data, not the DAX-based row-level security defined inside a Power BI semantic model. The two are parallel mechanisms at different layers, and mixing them up is exactly the distinction this chapter draws between model-level security and OneLake-level security.

questions.prompt: A user holds a workspace Viewer role on a report, and an admin also previously granted them a direct item-level permission on that same report. An admin now revokes only the item-level permission, leaving the Viewer role in place. What happens?
options: The user can still open the report — the workspace Viewer role alone is enough to see it exists and view it, so removing only the item permission doesn't cut off access
The user immediately loses all access to the report, since the item-level permission was the one actually granting visibility
The user can still edit the report, since the workspace role always takes priority over an item-level grant
An error occurs, because a workspace role and an item-level permission can't coexist on the same item
questions.explain: Lesson 11 documents this exact consequence: a workspace role and a direct item permission are two independent grants, and either one alone can be enough to view an item. Removing only the item permission leaves the workspace Viewer role intact, which already grants the ability to see the report exists and open it. Fully cutting off access requires removing both the item permission and the workspace role.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about row-level security (RLS) and object-level security (OLS) in Fabric, per Lesson 12.
options: RLS only restricts Viewers — workspace Admins, Members, and Contributors bypass it entirely and always see every row
OLS hides entire tables or columns from a role, so members can't see them in the field list or query them through Q&A or Copilot
OLS can be authored directly in the Fabric portal, the same way RLS roles are created in Power BI Desktop
Role definitions and DAX filters are created in Power BI Desktop, but members are assigned to a role afterward, in the Power BI service
RLS automatically hides a table's existence from a role, the same way OLS does
questions.explain: RLS restricts only Viewers, since Admins, Members, and Contributors already have full access to the underlying data regardless. OLS hides tables or columns from a role's visibility entirely. Roles and DAX filters are defined in Power BI Desktop, but members can't be assigned from Desktop — that happens afterward, in the service. OLS has no native authoring surface in the Fabric portal or Power BI Desktop at all; it requires an external tool like Tabular Editor or the XMLA endpoint. RLS also doesn't hide a table's existence — it filters rows while leaving the table itself structurally visible, which is exactly the gap OLS exists to close.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: row-level security directly on a Fabric Warehouse table is implemented with the T-SQL statement CREATE SECURITY ________, which attaches a filter predicate function to a target table.
questions.explain: CREATE SECURITY POLICY adds a filter predicate function (built with CREATE FUNCTION ... WITH SCHEMABINDING) onto a table, enforcing row-level security directly at the Warehouse/SQL analytics endpoint layer — independent of, and not automatically inherited by, any Power BI semantic model built on top.

questions.prompt: Match each Purview sensitivity-label concept to what it actually does, per Lessons 13-14.
right: A new report built on an already-labeled semantic model picks up that label immediately, whether or not the other propagation setting is enabled
Pre-fills new, unlabeled Fabric and Power BI content with a starting label the moment it's created
Automatic propagation of a label from a semantic model or report to everything already built on top of it, without overwriting a manual label or downgrading one
Blocks saving changes to an item at all until a label is applied to it
questions.explain: A default label policy pre-fills new content with a starting label; a mandatory label policy blocks saving until something is labeled. Downstream inheritance propagates an existing label to everything already built on top, without ever overwriting a manual choice or weakening it. Inheritance upon creation is a different mechanism entirely — a brand-new item built on already-labeled content inherits that label the instant it's created, regardless of whether downstream inheritance is even turned on.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of searching the Fabric/Power BI audit log in the correct order, per Lesson 15.
items: A Fabric tenant admin turns on auditing in the Fabric/Power BI admin portal
An investigator opens the Microsoft Purview portal at purview.microsoft.com/audit, not a Fabric-specific screen
The investigator sets a date range and optionally narrows by specific users or activities, then submits the search
The search runs as a background job and lands on the Audit search job dashboard
The investigator opens the completed job to review one row per audit event, filter columns, or export to CSV
questions.explain: Auditing has to be turned on tenant-wide before any events get captured. From there, a search is run from the unified Microsoft Purview portal — never a Fabric-only screen — with a date range and optional user/activity filters, submitted as a background job that lands on the search dashboard once complete, where the actual row-by-row results can be filtered or exported.

questions.prompt: An organization's content happens to match the auto-labeling conditions of both its General label (priority 1) and its Highly Confidential label (priority 4) at the same time. Which label does Microsoft Purview actually apply, and why?
options: Highly Confidential — Purview always resolves a conflict between matching labels by applying the one with the highest priority number
General — Purview always applies whichever label was created first, regardless of priority number
Both labels are applied simultaneously, since Fabric allows a single item to carry more than one sensitivity label
Neither — a conflict between two matching labels causes the content to remain unlabeled until an admin manually resolves it
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit about the convention and the resolution rule: least-restrictive labels sit at the top of the priority list with the lowest number, most-restrictive at the bottom with the highest, and when content matches more than one label's conditions, Purview always applies the one with the highest priority number — Highly Confidential here, at priority 4.

questions.prompt: A report author finds three semantic models in the catalog that all claim to calculate 'revenue.' One carries a Certified badge; the other two carry no badge at all. What does that Certified badge actually tell the author, per Lesson 18?
options: That model has been reviewed by a member of a security group a Fabric admin specifically authorized to certify content, and it meets the organization's quality and governance bar — not just one person's opinion
The model's own owner personally vouches for it being ready for others to use, the same self-service signal as a Promoted badge
The model is the authoritative, single source of truth for a core business entity like customers or product codes
The model has passed an automated data-quality scan with no manual review involved
questions.explain: Certified is a much stronger signal than Promoted — applying it is restricted to members of an admin-authorized security group, and it means the item has been reviewed against the organization's quality and governance bar, not just the creator's own judgment. Option B describes Promoted, which anyone with write access can self-apply with no review step. Option C describes the separate, even stricter Master Data tier.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Fabric's lineage view, per Lesson 19.
options: Every workspace has a lineage view automatically, with no setup or extra licensing required
A Viewer can open lineage view, but specifically does not see data source cards
Lineage view renders downstream items that live in a different workspace, the same as items in the current one
An arrow from Card A to Card B means data flows from A into B — A is upstream of B
A warning triangle next to a card's refresh timestamp flags a refresh that failed or needs attention
questions.explain: Lineage view is automatic and free on every workspace, arrows show direction (A upstream of B), and a warning triangle flags a failed or stalled refresh right on the card. A Viewer can open the diagram but is deliberately blocked from seeing data source cards. What lineage view does not do is render downstream items living in a different workspace — it only renders one workspace's graph plus external upstream sources one step back; tracing a ripple into other workspaces is exactly the job impact analysis exists for instead.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the impact analysis pane has two tabs for slicing the same result — Child Items, showing only items one step away, and ________, which expands that to every affected item further down the chain, including other workspaces.
questions.explain: Child Items shows only direct dependents; All downstream items expands the same result set to every item further down the chain, however many hops away, including items in entirely different workspaces — each tab reports its own count of affected items and workspaces.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the OneLake catalog to what it's actually for, per Lesson 17.
right: A unified view of workspace roles and OneLake security roles, for auditing and managing permissions
Find, browse, and inspect the Fabric items you have access to, or can request access to
Overview, Lineage, Monitor, and Permissions tabs for one selected item
Governance insights, recommended actions, and administrative settings for the data you own or the whole estate
questions.explain: Explore is the browse and discovery surface; Govern surfaces governance health and admin settings; Secure gives a unified view of workspace and OneLake security roles for auditing; and selecting any item opens its own detail pane with Overview, Lineage, Monitor, and Permissions tabs.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of running impact analysis and warning affected teams in the correct order, per Lesson 20.
items: Open impact analysis from an item's lineage-view card icon or its details page's Lineage dropdown
Switch between the Child Items and All downstream items tabs to see how far the change ripples
Browse the results by item type or by workspace to understand who's actually affected
Select Notify contacts and write a message describing the planned change
Send the notification, which reaches the contact lists of every impacted workspace, even ones you can't access
questions.explain: Impact analysis opens from either the lineage-view card icon or the item's own details page, then the Child Items / All downstream items tabs and the Browse-by-type / Browse-by-workspace views let you understand the real blast radius before touching anything. Only after seeing that does Notify contacts make sense — it emails a description of the change to every impacted workspace's contact list, even ones the sender personally can't access.

questions.prompt: An analyst with write permission runs impact analysis on a semantic model and sees several downstream items labeled 'Limited access' instead of their real names. Why?
options: Those items live in workspaces the analyst doesn't have access to, and Fabric withholds their real names because an item's name can itself expose information the analyst isn't permitted to see
Impact analysis has a hard cap on how many item names it can display, and 'Limited access' is shown once that cap is reached
The analyst needs write permission specifically on each downstream item, not just the original item, to see any name at all
'Limited access' means the item was deleted after impact analysis last ran
questions.explain: Impact analysis's privacy rule is specific: you only see real names for workspaces and items you personally have access to. Anything downstream you can't access shows as 'Limited access' instead of its actual name, precisely because an item's name can itself carry sensitive information that shouldn't be exposed to someone without permission on it — notification still reaches those workspaces' contact lists regardless, even though the analyst never learns the real names.

questions.prompt: A colleague has Read access to a published report built on a semantic model but wants to build their own new report directly against that model. Which permission do they need, and what does it specifically let them do?
options: Build — it lets them create new reports directly against the model, without being able to edit the model's measures or data sources
Reshare — it lets them grant Read access to other people without needing the model's owner involved
Read — the same permission they already have is sufficient to build new reports against the model
A workspace Contributor role, since Build isn't a real semantic-model permission
questions.explain: Lesson 21 lists three real permission levels on a semantic model: Read (view content built against it), Build (create new reports directly against it), and Reshare (grant Read to others). Read alone only lets someone view existing content like a published report; it doesn't let them build anything new against the model themselves, which is exactly why Build is a separate, more deliberate grant.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Fabric's three endorsement levels, per Lesson 22.
options: Promoted can be self-applied by any owner or anyone with write permission on the item, with no review step
Certified requires review by someone on an admin-authorized security group — never just the item owner's own personal judgment
Master Data is reserved for items that actually hold data, like lakehouses, warehouses, and semantic models — a report or dashboard can't carry it
Any item's owner can apply Certified to their own item purely by virtue of being the owner, with no admin authorization needed
Whether certification is enabled tenant-wide, and who's authorized to certify, is controlled centrally by a Fabric admin
questions.explain: Promoted is genuinely self-service — any write-permission holder can apply it with no review. Certified always requires being part of an admin-authorized security group; the owner's own opinion is never sufficient by itself. Master Data is reserved for items that actually hold data, so a report or dashboard can't carry it. Certification itself is a tenant-wide admin decision, enabled or disabled and scoped to specific authorized groups from the admin portal. Owning an item never grants Certified by itself — an owner can only certify their own item if they also happen to be on the authorized list, which is exactly why option D is false even though option B is true.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when Microsoft Purview and the Fabric tenant being scanned sit in the same tenant, the simplest scan credential is ________ — Purview's own managed identity, requiring no secrets to manage.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 names this directly: for a same-tenant setup, Microsoft Purview MSI (system) — Purview's own managed identity — is the simplest credential, with no secrets to manage. A dedicated service principal is the alternative, used for cross-tenant setups or when a narrower, more auditable identity is wanted instead.

questions.prompt: Match each Purview-Fabric scanning concept to what it actually is, per Lesson 23.
right: A dedicated, narrower identity used for cross-tenant scans or tighter auditing, requiring an app registration and granted API permissions
The process that reads a registered source's metadata into Purview's catalog
Keeps Purview's picture of the Fabric estate current automatically, with every scan after the first run incrementally
Purview's own managed identity, the simplest credential for a same-tenant scan with no secrets to manage
questions.explain: A scan is the metadata-reading process itself. Microsoft Purview MSI is the simplest same-tenant credential, needing no secrets. A service principal is the narrower, auditable alternative for cross-tenant setups, requiring an app registration and granted API permissions. A Recurring trigger keeps the catalog current automatically, with the first scan always full and every one after that incremental.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of registering and scanning a Fabric tenant into Microsoft Purview in the correct order, per Lesson 23.
items: Register the Fabric tenant as a data source in Microsoft Purview
Decide whether to include or exclude personal workspaces from the scan
Choose the scan's credential — Microsoft Purview MSI for a same-tenant setup, or a dedicated service principal otherwise
Set the scan trigger to Once for a single pass or Recurring to keep the catalog current automatically
Let the first scan run as a full scan, with every subsequent recurring scan running incrementally
questions.explain: Registering the Fabric tenant as a source comes first, then the personal-workspaces include/exclude decision and the credential choice are both configured as part of setting up the scan itself, then the trigger decides whether it runs once or repeats — and whichever trigger is chosen, the very first scan is always full, with every later one incremental.

questions.prompt: Northfield Health Network's six hospital sites each had their own version of 'Patient Readmission Rate.' After applying this course's governance controls, the compliance audit found one traceable answer. What was actually different about the fix, per Lesson 24?
options: Every governance layer — domains, a shared Lakehouse instead of six copies, row-level security, a certified semantic model, and a Purview scan — pointed at the same single definition, rather than any one Fabric feature being used in isolation
Fabric automatically merged the six different definitions into one correct average the moment Purview scanned the tenant
The audit accepted all six definitions as valid, since each hospital site's workspace had its own activity log
A tenant admin manually deleted five of the six semantic models so only one definition could exist
questions.explain: The case study's actual point isn't any single feature — it's that domains, a shared Lakehouse with a shortcut instead of duplicated data, row-level security, sensitivity labels, certification, and a Purview scan all got pointed at the same one definition. That's why the audit got a traceable answer: not because the underlying numbers were reconciled after the fact, but because every layer of the course was already aimed at a single source before the audit ever asked.
